sections.title: 英语知识运用
sections.directions: Directions: Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: Most of us strive for self-respect — to see ourselves in a positive light, to be
of who we are. Any comments or experiences that undermine those feelings of self-worth can be uncomfortable and it's only
to want to avoid them. But the thing is,
your self-worth really is being undermined is, to a large degree, subjective. Much of it comes down to your

of what someone said or did. When you take things personally, you're interpreting these situations as saying something significant and negative about you as a person. Say your boss picks holes in your sales report, and you come away feeling like this means she thinks you're a
member of staff. Or, two of your friends cancel your
get- together at the pub and you interpret this as meaning they're bored of you. Psychologists have a
for this way of thinking: personalisation. But the
is that your boss might view you very highly. It's just you made some
in the report and she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time.
, in the case of your friends cancelling, perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend or they just
their minds. In both
— and others that we all experience — there's another
at work that psychologists call mind reading. This is when you assume to know what other people are thinking about you, when you can't really know without
them directly. One simple way to avoid
personalisation and mind reading is to challenge your negative assumptions of what's
. When you find yourself taking a situation personally, try to think of other interpretations that are less focused on you — especially in the sense of saying anything deep or
about you. When you do this, it might help to try to put yourself in other people's shoes. The fact your boss took the time to give you
at all means they care enough to want to help you
. When it comes to your friends — maybe it's because your friendship is so
that they felt able to cancel at late notice.

questions.analysis: proud 【线索】self-respect 与正面光下 本句关键正向词链是 self-respect 和 to see ourselves in a positive light，明确这是正面 感受。紧随其后的 to be __(1)__ of who we are 与之并列，所填词必须延续"正面看待自 【选项】A) afraid ✗ 色彩相反 afraid 表"害怕"，与 self-respect、positive light 构成的正向链冲突，be afraid of who we are B) critical ✗ 态度偏负 critical 是"挑剔/批判"，be critical of who we are 即"挑剔自己是谁"，与开头追求 self-respect C) proud ✓ 正向且固定搭配 be proud of 是固定搭配，意为"为……感到自豪"，与 to see ourselves in a positive light 同向 并列，完美承接 self-respect 的正面色彩。 D) tolerant ✗ 强度不足且跑偏 tolerant 是"容忍"，be tolerant of who we are 意为"容忍自己是谁"，含"勉强接受"意味，与"自 【验证】代回后 to be __(1)__ of who we are 即 to be proud of who we are，与 to see ourselves in a positive light 并列同义，整段开篇"人都追求自我尊重——以正面眼光看自

natural 【线索】only 暗示理所应当 Any comments or experiences that undermine those feelings of self-worth can be uncomfortable and it's only __(2)__ to want to avoid them. 中 only 是关键，only + 形 【选项】A) risky ✗ 评价偏负 But the thing is 的反转点不构成正常铺垫。 B) natural ✓ 贴合 only 合理化语气 it's only natural to do 是英语高频表达，意为"想……再自然不过"，正好把作者"先承认人之常 C) admirable ✗ 褒义过头 D) foolish ✗ 贬义且与 only 冲突 【验证】代回 it's only __(2)__ to want to avoid them 即 it's only natural to want to avoid them，意为"想避开（让人不适的言论）再自然不过"，与紧随其后的 But the thing is 形

whether 【线索】主观与否而非地点原因 主句宾语是 to a large degree, subjective——"在很大程度上是主观的"。判断对象只能 【选项】 A) whether ✓ 是否真的受损 large degree, subjective 这个真假判断维度。 B) where ✗ 无地点缺口 where 需要从句缺地点状语，但 your self-worth really is being undermined 在语义上不需要地 C) why ✗ 主观针对真假非原因 D) how ✗ 方式与判断错配 【验证】代回 __(3)__ your self-worth really is being undermined is, to a large degree, it comes down to your __(4)__ of what someone said or did. 中的"很大程度上取决于你

perception 【线索】subjective 锁定主观解读 前句 is, to a large degree, subjective 与本句 Much of it comes down to your __(4)__ 由 Much of it 串起，it 指代上句"自我价值是否被冒犯"。subjective 一词锁定填空词必须指 向"个人主观加工"——只有 perception（看法、感知）契合，引文也明确针对的是 what someone said or did——他人的言行。 【选项】A) citation ✗ 意为引用偏离 B) imitation ✗ 模仿对象错位 imitation 表"模仿"，your imitation of what someone said 意为"你对别人话的模仿"，但语境 C) perception ✓ 主观感知正解 perception 表"看法、感知"，your perception of what someone said or did 正好是"你对别 D) introduction ✗ 搭配语义不通 【验证】代回 Much of it comes down to your __(4)__ of what someone said or did. 即"这（自 清晰的因果/同义链；为第二段进一步阐述 personalisation 做铺垫。

poor 【线索】picks holes 锁定负评 前文 your boss picks holes in your sales report——pick holes in 是"挑刺、挑毛病"的固 定表达，触发事件是"被挑错"，由此你才会 come away feeling like 老板觉得你是个"差劲 的"员工。线索就在本句内的 picks holes。 【选项】 A) poor ✓ 差劲与挑刺呼应 poor 表"差劲的、不胜任的"，a poor member of staff 即"一个不合格的员工"，与 picks holes in your sales report 的负面色彩一致。 B) loyal ✗ 色彩相反 C) creative ✗ 褒义不符 D) shy ✗ 维度跑偏 【验证】代回 she thinks you're a __(5)__ member of staff 即"她觉得你是个差劲的员工"，与 picks holes in your sales report 触发的负面自我解读一致，作为 personalisation 的典型例证逻

planned 【线索】cancel 暗示已有约定 本句关键动词 cancel 是"取消"；能被取消的 get-together 一定是事先"已计划好的"。线索 【选项】A) sponsored ✗ 赞助维度跑偏 B) crowded ✗ 形容场地非聚会 crowded 是"拥挤的"，多形容场所人多；用来形容 get-together 本身不自然，也与"被取消"无逻 C) disputed ✗ 争议含义不符 D) planned ✓ 计划与取消天然搭 planned 是"已计划好的"，cancel a planned get-together 是英语典型搭配，且只有事先"约 【验证】代回 cancel your __(6)__ get-together at the pub 即"取消你们已约好的酒吧小聚"，与下 文 you interpret this as meaning they're bored of you 形成完整故事——本来说好的聚

term 【线索】冒号后 personalisation 是术语 【选项】A) method ✗ 方法非名称 method 是"方法"，但冒号后 personalisation 是一个名词性的称呼而非一套做法，对不上。 B) term ✓ 术语正解 term 表"术语、名称"，have a term for X 是英语固定表达"对 X 有个专门叫法"，与冒号后给出 的术语 personalisation 完全对应。 C) design ✗ 设计与命名无关 design 是"设计"，心理学家不会去"设计"一种思维方式，搭配 have a design for 也不通顺。 D) goal ✗ 目标偏离 goal 是"目标"，心理学家对这种思维的"目标"在此完全没必要讨论，且 a goal for this way of thinking 语义混乱。 【验证】代回 Psychologists have a __(7)__ for this way of thinking: personalisation. 即"心理学

reality 【线索】But 引出与前文相反的真相 But the __(8)__ is 中 But 把第二段你以为的"老板嫌弃你"翻转过来，引出 your boss might view you very highly——这是事实层面的真相，与前一段你脑补的"想法"对立。该词要承 【选项】A) evidence ✗ 证据需有出处 evidence 是"证据"，需依托具体来源；后文 your boss might view you very highly 是一种可能 性陈述而非证据材料，搭配 the evidence is that 不自然。 B) theory ✗ 理论与可能错位 theory 是"理论"，但后文 your boss might view you very highly 是对实际情况的猜测，不是理 C) condition ✗ 条件与真相无关 D) reality ✓ 真相一锤定音 reality 是"现实、真相"，But the reality is that... 是英语表"但事实是……"的高频结构，正好与第 【验证】代回 But the __(8)__ is that your boss might view you very highly. 即"但事实是，你的 老板可能对你评价很高"，与第二段 she thinks you're a __(5)__ member of staff 你脑补的

mistakes 【线索】point these out 反推 mistakes 本句后半 she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time——老板 holes in your sales report 也呼应"挑出毛病"。 【选项】A) complaints ✗ 抱怨方向反 B) choices ✗ 中性不触发指正 C) mistakes ✓ 错误指出最常配 mistakes 是"错误"，make mistakes 是固定搭配；point out 错误以便"do better next time"逻 D) suggestions ✗ 建议来源错位 suggestions 是"建议"，但 you made suggestions in the report 表示"你在报告里给出了建 【验证】代回 It's just you made some __(9)__ in the report 即"只是你在报告里犯了一些错"，与 she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time 形成"犯错—指出—下

Similarly 【线索】老板事例与朋友事例平行 前半段刚分析完老板这例的真相（your boss might view you very highly），本句切到 in the case of your friends cancelling, perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend or they just __(11)__ their minds.——同样给出"真相另解"。两件事是"两个事例平行展开"， 【选项】 A) Similarly ✓ 类比并列恰当 Similarly 是"同样地"，正好把老板事例和朋友事例两种 personalisation 的真相做平行对照—— B) Relatively ✗ 相对偏离 C) Accordingly ✗ 因果不成立 D) Contrarily ✗ 对立关系反方向 【验证】代回 __(10)__, in the case of your friends cancelling 即"同样地，就朋友取消聚会这件事

changed 【线索】cancel 与 change one's mind both felt unwell that weekend），or 后再给一种"无理由地变卦"。change one's mind 【选项】A) opened ✗ 搭配不解释取消 opened 与 minds 搭配是 open one's mind"打开思路、接受新事物"，无法解释"为何取消 聚会"。 B) changed ✓ 改变主意正解 changed 与 minds 构成 change one's mind"改变主意"，正好解释朋友"临时变卦取消聚会"的 C) trained ✗ 训练大脑跑偏 trained 与 minds 搭配是 train one's mind"训练大脑"，多用于自我提升语境，与取消聚会无关。 D) cleared ✗ 清空思绪偏离 cleared 与 minds 搭配是 clear one's mind"清空思绪"，多指放空、冥想，与"取消聚会"没有解释 【验证】代回 they just __(11)__ their minds 即"他们只是改变了主意"，与前半 perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend 用 or 并列，给出朋友取消聚会的两种合理真相，逻辑顺畅。

examples 【线索】老板与朋友是两个例子 前两段铺开的两件事 your boss picks holes in your sales report 与 two of your friends cancel your __(6)__ get-together at the pub 是用来说明 personalisation 的具体生活事 例；in both ___ 自然指"在这两个例子中"。本句 others that we all experience 也补充支 【选项】A) quotations ✗ 引文性质不符 B) experiments ✗ 实验语境错配 C) questions ✗ 问题层级跑偏 questions 是"问题"，但前文不是抛出问题而是描述场景；in both questions 也不符合英语 D) examples ✓ 例子最贴语境 examples 是"例子"，in both examples 直接呼应前文老板和朋友这两个 personalisation 的生 【验证】代回 In both __(12)__ — and others that we all experience 即"在这两个例子——以及

process 【线索】personalisation 是 process 的并列 第二段 Psychologists have a __(7)__ for this way of thinking: personalisation.—— personalisation 被定义为"a way of thinking"，是一种心理过程。本段 another __(13)__ at work 中 another 暗示与之同类，psychologists call mind reading 也对应 way of thinking 这一性质。 【选项】 A) process ✓ 心理过程对应思维方式 process 是"过程"，与第二段 this way of thinking 同类——personalisation 和 mind reading B) objective ✗ 目标性质不符 objective 是"目标、目的"，但 mind reading 是一种思维活动而不是一个目标，对不上。 C) outcome ✗ 结果偏离过程 outcome 是"结果"，是事后产物；mind reading 是发生中的思维活动，需要的是"过程"而 非"结果"。 D) background ✗ 背景性质错位 background 是"背景"，是静态情景而非心理活动；不能用 at work 描述"在起作用"。 【验证】代回 there's another __(13)__ at work that psychologists call mind reading 即"还有另

asking 【线索】知道别人想法靠直接问 本句前半 you assume to know what other people are thinking about you, when you can't really know without __(14)__ them directly——核心是"真正知道别人在想什么"， 【选项】A) blaming ✗ 指责非获知途径 B) warning ✗ 警告与求知无关 C) teaching ✗ 教导而非询问 D) asking ✓ 直接询问最直接 asking 是"询问"，是直接获知对方想法的最直接方式，与 directly 完美呼应；ask sb directly 也 【验证】代回 you can't really know without __(14)__ them directly 即"不直接问对方就真的没法

engaging in 【线索】personalisation 是心理活动 宾语 personalisation and mind reading 都是"思维方式/心理活动"。本段后文 When you find yourself taking a situation personally 也表明这是"卷入这种思维"而不是"讨论或解 【选项】A) arguing about ✗ 争论方向跑偏 arguing about 是"争论"，意味把 personalisation 当成话题去吵；但作者要避免的是"陷入这种思 B) accounting for ✗ 解释非陷入 accounting for 是"解释、说明"，但 avoid accounting for personalisation 意为"避免去解释 C) engaging in ✓ 陷入思维活动正解 engaging in 是"参与、陷入"，engage in personalisation and mind reading 表"陷入这两种 D) interfering with ✗ 干扰对象不符 interfering with 是"干扰、妨碍"，意味把 personalisation 当成被妨碍的事物；但作者不是要去干 【验证】代回 One simple way to avoid __(15)__ personalisation and mind reading 即"避免陷入 personalisation 和 mind reading 的一种简单方法"，与下句 When you find yourself taking a situation personally 描述"卷入思维"的场景对应，承接段落"给对策"的功能。

happened 【线索】negative assumptions 的对象 challenge your negative assumptions of what's __(16)__——前文反复举的事件都是"已 经发生"的事（老板挑了你的报告，朋友取消了聚会）；assumptions of what's 【选项】 A) happened ✓ 对发生事件最贴 happened 表"已发生的事"，what's happened 即"发生了什么"，正好对应前文事例——你 B) continued ✗ 持续性偏题 C) returned ✗ 回归与情境无关 D) disappeared ✗ 消失方向不符 【验证】代回 challenge your negative assumptions of what's __(16)__ 即"挑战你对所发生之事的 other interpretations 形成"挑战旧解—换新解"的连贯逻辑。

fundamental 【线索】deep 锁定根本性 saying anything deep or __(17)__ about you 中 deep 表"深层的、深刻的"，意指关于 【选项】A) casual ✗ 随意与深刻相反 B) obvious ✗ 明显非深刻 C) familiar ✗ 熟悉与深刻错位 D) fundamental ✓ 根本性与深刻同向 【验证】代回 saying anything deep or __(17)__ about you 即"说出关于你的任何深层或根本性的

feedback 【线索】picks holes + point out 即 feedback 回看前文 your boss picks holes in your sales report 与 she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time——老板挑出问题并指给你看，让你下次改进，正是英语 里 feedback"反馈"的标准定义。 【选项】A) reward ✗ 奖赏方向错 B) feedback ✓ 反馈一锤定音 feedback 是"反馈"，give sb feedback 是工作场景的固定搭配；老板挑错并指出问题正是反馈 的内容，下文 want to help you __(19)__ 也呼应反馈的目的。 C) trust ✗ 信任范畴跑偏 D) proof ✗ 证据维度错位 proof 是"证据"，老板不会"给你证据"，搭配 give you proof 在此语境不通顺。 【验证】代回 your boss took the time to give you __(18)__ at all 即"老板愿意花时间给你反馈"， 与前文老板"挑错并指出来"的动作正好对应；与下句 they care enough to want to help you __(19)__ 中"想帮你改进"形成"反馈—助改进"的因果链。

improve 【线索】feedback + do better 锁 improve 上文 so that you do better next time 已经明示反馈目的是"下次做得更好"；本句 help you __(19)__ 与之同义换说，自然填 improve"改进、进步"。 【选项】A) innovate ✗ 创新过窄 B) concentrate ✗ 专注偏题 C) improve ✓ 改进与 do better 等价 improve 是"改进、进步"，正好与上文 do better next time 同义；help you improve 是英语 D) relax ✗ 放松方向反 【验证】代回 they care enough to want to help you __(19)__ 即"他们足够在乎你、想帮你进 步"，与前文 so that you do better next time 同义换说，全段把老板挑错重新解读为"善

strong 【线索】敢临时取消因关系牢固 that they felt able to cancel at late notice 提示前面填空词要解释"为何朋友才敢临时放鸽 【选项】A) strange ✗ 古怪不合逻辑 B) strong ✓ 牢固关系敢取消 strong 是"牢固的"，a strong friendship 表"关系够牢固"——这种关系下临时取消不会被视为 绝交信号，正好让朋友 felt able to cancel at late notice，因果链顺畅，且与全文给读者宽慰的 C) vulnerable ✗ 脆弱与取消因果反 D) valuable ✗ 宝贵不直接导致敢取消 【验证】代回 your friendship is so __(20)__ that they felt able to cancel at late notice 即"你们 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 避免的方法。开篇 Most of us strive for self-respect — to see ourselves in a positive light 定调话题是自我价值感与对外界评价的反应，Much of it comes down to your __(4)__ of what someone said or did. 则点明核心立场——感受被冒犯往往源于自己的解读。 文章按四步推进：第一段 to a large degree, subjective 提出自我价值受损在很大程度上是 主观解读；第二段用两个生活例子（your boss picks holes in your sales report 与 two of your friends cancel your __(6)__ get-together at the pub）说明什么叫 personalisation；第 三段以 But the __(8)__ is 反转，给出 your boss might view you very highly 等真实可能；第 四段 there's another __(13)__ at work that psychologists call mind reading 引出第二个概 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 11 Most of us strive for self-respect — to see ourselves in a positive light, to be proud of who we are. Any comments or experiences that undermine those feelings of self-worth can be uncomfortable and it's only natural to want to avoid them. But the thing is, whether your self-worth really is being undermined is, to a large degree, subjective. Much of it comes down to your perception of what someone said or did. sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Ask people about public libraries and a certain image springs to mind: dusty, old-fashioned, the sort of place you enjoyed as a child but, rather like a British seaside town, would you go there now? And anyway — aren't they all closing? The reality is startlingly different, as I discovered when the culture department commissioned me to conduct an independent review of English public libraries, published yesterday. As I visited libraries up and down the country, I was surprised to learn there are more than twice the number of libraries (2,892) as there are branches of McDonald's. Enter any one of them and you will find a hive of activity. While books are, and should always be, at the heart of any library, a multitude of other services are offered: employment advice, language classes or digital access and support. There are libraries with business and intellectual property centres, which can help business owners and entrepreneurs. Many have nurses on site to carry out basic health checks, with a link to the GP's surgery. There are libraries where young people can borrow a Fifa-standard football free. In return for all of this, you'll be asked for precisely nothing. There will be no charge and you will never be asked to justify or explain yourself; you will simply be welcomed in, offered help if you need it, and left alone if you do not. There is no other institution, public or private, that can say the same. Yet still our libraries are often overlooked and underappreciated. There is an overall decline in visits and many are struggling as local authorities come under continued financial pressure. The number of libraries that have closed since 2010 is disputed. An annual survey by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy puts it at nearly 800 across the UK; official statistics held by the Arts Council record 230 in England. It is, of course, 230 libraries too many. So if we are to protect our libraries for future generations, we must raise awareness of them and the work they do. The review recommends a national branding campaign to give libraries a stronger physical presence, the reintroduction of a scheme to enable members to use their card in any library in the country, and automatic memberships for children. If we don't use them, we will end up losing them. And for those who haven't been to a library for some time, they may be surprised by what they find.

According to our research, around one in five workers in the UK talk to AI like a friend, looking for guidance on personal and professional problems. Our data shows that engaging with AI like this can leave us feeling heard and less isolated. But, with this newfound connection, many of us share sensitive, sometimes highly confidential information, even though over a third of people don't realise that AI platforms may not be very good at keeping our secrets…secret. For businesses, the implications are worrying. Consider Microsoft Copilot, for example. It gains Microsoft broad rights to the data inputted or outputted by any user — rights to use this data in any way it sees fit; it can even share it with third parties. This means that any sensitive business information could potentially be exposed to the world. Employers are taking note and taking action. According to our research, 25% have decided to either outright ban AI or regulate its use within their organisations. But even with these policies in place, some employees choose to break the rules. They have their reasons — around 63% of them report that using AI increases their productivity, and some even feel AI offers more help than their human colleagues. The situation presents a delicate balance between leveraging AI for its productivity gains and risking confidential data exposure. Employers need to manage AI tools with the same level of care as any other form of data sharing or storage. There's also a knowledge gap that needs to be addressed — 40% of individuals surveyed are unsure about who retains ownership over the content produced by AI. By instilling best practices in AI engagement and creating policies that evolve with the technology, businesses can positively shift the AI landscape. With AI's potential to simplify our professional lives, do the admin and enhance the work experience, it's up to us to navigate its usage cautiously so it supports us without compromising our privacy. There's no need to back away from progress, as long as we're equipped with the knowledge and tools to make sure AI remains a friend. And this is where the challenge lies. There are so many products out there, being promoted with huge advertising and marketing budgets, that it's easy to fall victim. But by building a culture of digital responsibility within our businesses, we can create a future where AI can help us without spilling the beans.

Since the 2008 launch of the high-speed rail network between Rome and Milan, trains have become the preferred means of travel across Italy for locals and tourists alike. Fast trains can cover the 500km between the two cities in three hours. The network also connects Naples, Bologna, Florence and Turin. In many cases, it is the best option — in terms of travel time and cost — for both leisure and business travellers. This is why the recent severe delays caused by numerous maintenance works have thrown the rail industry into chaos at a time when most people head on holiday, which matters for business in a country where tourism accounts for 10 percent of GDP. Disruptions have become increasingly frequent with train delays now a fixture in Italian media coverage. Ferrovie dello Stato Italiane, the publicly controlled group that owns train operator Trenitalia and the national train network RFI, said 23 percent of all high-speed trains it operated were late in 2023. The huge improvements in Italy's obsolete infrastructure partly explained the disruption, said Ferrovie. RFI, the network operator, is the single largest European recovery fund beneficiary with planned investments of €24bn by 2026. Ferrovie will invest a total of €124bn in infrastructure over the next 10 years. But lack of capacity is another problem. Transport economist Andrea Giuricin said the planned investments would bring improvements but disruptions in the meantime were inevitable. "We have a mixed system, there is no spare capacity and as soon as there's a hiccup on the line, the situation becomes highly complex," he said. A mixed system means that high-speed trains must travel on the regular tracks on certain routes or when passing through large cities. If there's congestion or, for example, a local train breaks down, the entire high-speed network is affected. One of the most important changes the upgrades will bring is the segregation of the high-speed line from the regular one in certain urban centres through the construction of underground rail links. Improvements will also come from the high-density technology and satellite signalling that RFI has been investing in for years, say experts. It will allow for a reduction of the distance between high-speed trains travelling on the same line at any given time, which should mean a significant increase in capacity and traffic fluidity, according to Giuricin.

In 2023, Chicago lost one of its most beloved street festivals. The Silver Room Block Party, staged by Hyde Park community leader Eric Williams, announced it would not return in 2024. What began as a small neighborhood gathering blossomed into a massive cultural event, welcoming tens of thousands of people each year over nearly two decades before abruptly shutting down. Williams pointed to rising production costs and declining attendee donations as primary reasons the Silver Room Block Party could not continue, highlighting a reality that all street festival organizers face right now. The cost of producing a street festival in Chicago has skyrocketed. Security, entertainment, portable restrooms, insurance and even basics such as fencing and staffing have all become significantly more expensive. At the same time, donations at festival gates have dropped dramatically. Chicago's summer festivals are about more than just entertainment; they are economic engines that directly benefit the neighborhoods they're in and the city of Chicago as a whole. Street festivals drive foot traffic to local businesses and foster the kind of cultural vibrancy that makes our city special. We often hear people ask why we solicit donations at our entry points, especially when the city's largest festivals like the Chicago Jazz Festival do not request donations. The fact is, unlike those large, city-produced music festivals, your neighborhood street festivals receive no city funding and rely on a combination of sponsorships, vendor fees and gate donations to cover their costs. Wicker Park Fest has long been one of Chicago's most anticipated summer festivals, drawing upward of 70,000 attendees for a full weekend of live indie music, local art, small business vendors and, most importantly, community connection. In 2024, Wicker Park Fest saw record-breaking attendance. Despite the turnout, gate donations reached their lowest point in our history. This year, we've been forced to scale back the footprint of the fest. We are eliminating a stage, booking fewer performers and making additional cuts to reduce our costs, all while striving to keep the festival as vibrant as ever, as supportive of local artists and businesses, and as true to Wicker Park's unique spirit and reputation as festgoers have come to expect. This summer, as you enjoy your favorite neighborhood street festival, I hope you'll remember that they exist because of community support. A thriving summer festival season doesn't happen by accident; it happens when we all chip in.

questions.question: The author holds that the future of street festivals depends on ____ Part B Directions: Read the following text and match each of the numbered items in the left column to its corresponding information in the right column. There are two extra choices in the right column. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points) In an effort to support restoration programmes, specialists are developing supplies of seeds and seedlings, maintaining gene banks and sequencing the genomes of indigenous trees and other crops. Their work deals with one of the problems that could block major restoration efforts in different parts of the world. "Where's the planting material going to come from? That's one big bottleneck," says genetic-resources specialist Ramni Jamnadass. Asia is arguably the region most neglected by global efforts to increase diversity in restoration and to study native species. Christopher Kettle, Biodiversity International's director for forest genetic resources and restoration in Rome, says that the need for infrastructure — things such as mechanisms for collecting and storing seeds, and nurseries to raise seedlings — might be most desperate here because many trees are 'masting' species, which don't produce seeds every year. People need to be ready. "Otherwise, you miss the boat, you lose all the seed and you've got to wait another seven years," says Kettle. "This is a really, really critical issue for restoration in Southeast Asia, because many of the most important timber species and tree species — the ones that will lock up the most carbon — they're all masting species." Climate change is a driving factor in the push to restore forests, but it also raises questions, such as where trees can thrive in the future. Climate change is also expected to alter relationships between trees, insects, diseases and other forest species. "Insects that today are a minor problem may become a major problem if they can produce three or four generations in a year," says forest ecologist John Stanturf. This remains a significant knowledge gap. "We know enough to know that this is a concern, but we don't know enough about how to respond to it yet. That's a great area to be doing research." So is soil, says Cindy Prescott, a forest ecologist at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. "If you don't look at the soil at the start, you can spend a lot of money and time putting in species that aren't going to survive there." With so much research left to do, leaders in the field have been doing some soul-searching, and acknowledging that restoration can be motivated by — and designed to meet — different needs. "When you talk about conservation or restoration, the first question has to be restoration by whom, for whom?" says Daniel Janzen, a biologist at the University of Pennsylvania. The question can have more than one answer. Much of the global funding for restoration is dedicated to developing it as a tool to mitigate climate change, notes restoration ecologist Pedro Brancalion. "But if you ask a farmer in Brazil if he or she is concerned about climate change, they would say, 'No, I am concerned about water,'" he says. Their interests as stewards of the land need to be better integrated with those who have the money to support restoration. That has been the strongest lesson of all for forest ecologist Robin Chazdon. Restoration is about more than what gets planted in the ground, she says. "Yes, it's about forests, but it's really about people. They are the agents of restoration." some kinds of trees do not produce seeds annually.
